claims.text: In sub-10 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles, surface-energy minimization dominates configurational-entropy stabilization.
The high surface-to-volume ratio creates a steep chemical-potential gradient between the core and surface.
The chemical-potential gradient favors segregation of Au and Cu to the nanoparticle surface.
The surface-driven segregation overrides the sluggish-diffusion behavior typically associated with bulk high-entropy alloys.
Au and Cu segregation lowers the total Gibbs free energy of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Surface-energy minimization drives reshaping from elliptical to spherical particles by reducing surface area.
Surface-segregated Au and Cu subsequently evaporate at elevated temperatures.
The initial particles are sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles synthesized by pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane.
The initial nanoparticles likely contain a high density of surface defects and nonequilibrium atomic arrangements.
For sub-5 nm particles, the surface term γA in G = G_bulk + γA dominates the configurational-entropy term TΔS_conf.
Au and Cu have significantly lower surface energies than Co, Ni, and Pt.
A high surface-defect concentration and short diffusion paths kinetically facilitate Au and Cu segregation.
Increasing the surface concentration of Au and Cu lowers their cohesive energy and raises their vapor pressure.
A rapid increase in surface Au and Cu concentration should occur above approximately 600–700 K.
Above the critical temperature, Au and Cu enrichment should be followed by measurable particle shrinkage and a transition to spherical morphology.
Smaller nanoparticles evaporate faster than larger nanoparticles, widening the particle-size distribution.
The proposed surface-energy mechanism is valid only for nanoparticles smaller than 10 nm.
For particles larger than 50 nm, bulk entropy stabilization and sluggish diffusion dominate and prevent segregation and evaporation.
Changing the initial shape between icosahedral and truncated-octahedral geometries can shift the critical temperature by approximately ±50 K.
The critical temperature depends on initial defect density, particle size, and the surface energies of the specific AuCoCuNiPt composition.
